course.title: Computer Networks
course.description: A structured Computer Networks course based on the Computer Networks Notes PDF.

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.description: Fundamentals of computer networks, protocols, network types, topologies and switching.

topics.title: What is a Computer Network?
topics.learn: A computer network is a group of interconnected nodes or devices that share resources and information through communication links.
topics.example: A laptop, smartphone and printer connected through a network can exchange data and share resources.
keyPoints: Networks allow resource and information sharing.

topics.title: Nodes
topics.learn: A node is a device capable of sending and receiving data. End nodes include PCs, printers, servers and smartphones. Intermediary nodes include routers, bridges and modems.
topics.example: A laptop can act as an end node while a router works as an intermediary node.
keyPoints: End nodes participate at the edge of communication.
Intermediary nodes help move or manage network traffic.

topics.title: Communication Links
topics.learn: A communication link is the medium used to transfer data between devices. Links may be wired or wireless.
topics.example: Ethernet or coaxial cable is a wired link, while Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are wireless links.
keyPoints: Wireless links use radio or other wireless communication.

topics.title: Uses and Services of Networks
topics.learn: Computer networks support communication, resource sharing, remote access and collaboration. They also provide services such as email, instant messaging, video telephony, storage, web browsing, file sharing and VoIP.
topics.example: Google Drive-style storage and online meetings depend on network communication.

topics.title: Characteristics of Computer Networks
topics.learn: Important characteristics include fault tolerance, scalability, quality of service and security.
topics.example: A scalable network can add devices without significantly degrading performance.

topics.title: Protocols
topics.learn: A protocol is a set of rules followed by communicating devices. Protocol information includes sender, receiver and communication media.
topics.example: HTTP defines rules used between web browsers and web servers.
keyPoints: Sender and receiver must follow compatible rules.

topics.title: Elements of a Protocol
topics.learn: Protocol elements include message encoding, message formatting and encapsulation, message timing, message size and message delivery options.
topics.example: A protocol can define how data is formatted before transmission and when it should be sent.

topics.title: Simplex, Half Duplex and Full Duplex
topics.learn: Simplex supports one-way communication. Half duplex supports two-way communication but only one direction at a time. Full duplex supports simultaneous two-way communication.
topics.example: A keyboard-to-CPU path represents simplex, a walkie-talkie represents half duplex, and a telephone call represents full duplex.
keyPoints: Half duplex = both directions, one at a time

topics.title: PAN, LAN, CAN, MAN and WAN
topics.learn: Networks can be classified by geographic range and use. The notes cover PAN, LAN, CAN, MAN and WAN.
topics.example: A LAN can connect computers within an office, while a WAN can connect networks across cities or countries.

topics.title: Client-Server and Peer-to-Peer Networks
topics.learn: A client-server model uses dedicated servers for centralized services and resource management. In a peer-to-peer network, systems can function as both clients and servers.
topics.example: An enterprise database commonly follows a client-server architecture, while file-sharing networks can use peer-to-peer communication.
keyPoints: P2P does not require a dedicated server

topics.title: Network Topology
topics.learn: Topology describes the layout and arrangement of nodes in a network. It can refer to physical placement or logical data flow.
topics.example: Two networks can have different physical arrangements while using similar logical communication behavior.

topics.title: Bus, Ring, Star, Mesh, Tree and Hybrid
topics.learn: The notes cover the structure, working, advantages, disadvantages and typical uses of six topology types.
topics.example: In star topology, devices connect to a central hub or switch. In mesh topology, devices have multiple direct paths.
keyPoints: Bus uses a shared central cable.

topics.title: Switching
topics.learn: Switching is a method of transmitting data between devices by selecting an available path. The notes cover circuit switching, message switching and packet switching.
topics.example: Traditional telephone networks use circuit switching, while modern data networks commonly use packet switching.

topics.title: Datagram and Virtual Circuit Approaches
topics.learn: The datagram approach is connectionless and allows packets to take different routes. The virtual circuit approach establishes a path before data transfer and keeps packets on the established route.
topics.example: The notes associate IP with the datagram approach and ATM/Frame Relay with the virtual circuit approach.
keyPoints: Virtual circuits use an established route

chapters.title: Devices
chapters.description: Network cables and important networking devices from the Physical, Data Link and Network layers.

topics.title: Network Cables
topics.learn: The notes cover Unshielded Twisted Pair, coaxial cable and fiber optic cable.
topics.example: Fiber optic communication sends data using light signals and supports long distances.

topics.title: Repeater
topics.learn: A repeater works at the Physical Layer and restores signal strength after attenuation. It forwards the signal without filtering it.
topics.example: A repeater can be placed along a long cable to regenerate a weakened signal.

topics.title: Repeater vs Amplifier
topics.learn: The notes distinguish a repeater, which restores the signal, from an amplifier, which boosts signal power and also amplifies noise.
topics.example: An amplifier can increase both the desired signal and existing noise.

topics.title: Hub
topics.learn: A hub works at the Physical Layer and acts as a multiport repeater. It broadcasts received data to connected devices.
topics.example: If a hub receives a frame on one port, it forwards the signal to the other connected ports.

topics.title: Bridge
topics.learn: A bridge works at the Data Link Layer and connects LAN segments. It uses MAC addresses and can filter traffic between segments.
topics.example: A bridge can avoid forwarding traffic to another segment when the destination is known to be on the same segment.

topics.title: Static and Dynamic Bridges
topics.learn: Static bridges use manually configured MAC address tables, while dynamic or transparent bridges learn addresses automatically.
topics.example: A transparent bridge can learn the location of devices from observed traffic.

topics.title: Switch
topics.learn: A switch operates at the Data Link Layer and functions like an advanced multiport bridge. It creates separate communication paths and supports full-duplex communication.
topics.example: A laptop, desktop and printer can communicate through separate switch ports.

topics.title: Router
topics.learn: A router operates at the Network Layer and forwards packets between networks using IP addresses and routing tables.
topics.example: A router can forward packets from a local network toward an Internet destination.

topics.title: Gateway
topics.learn: A gateway connects different networks and can translate between different network protocols. It can work across multiple OSI layers depending on the translation required.
topics.example: A VoIP gateway can connect IP-based networks with traditional telephone networks.

topics.title: Firewall
topics.learn: A firewall monitors and controls network traffic between trusted and untrusted networks using predefined rules.
topics.example: A firewall can filter traffic based on IP address, port or protocol.

topics.title: Intrusion Detection System
topics.learn: An IDS monitors network or system activity to identify suspicious behavior and generate alerts. The notes cover NIDS and HIDS.
topics.example: A NIDS can monitor traffic across a network while a HIDS monitors an individual host.

chapters.title: Physical Layer
chapters.description: The lowest OSI layer, transmission media, signaling and communication modes.

topics.title: Physical Layer Basics
topics.learn: The Physical Layer is the first layer from the bottom of the OSI model and handles transmission of raw bits.
topics.example: A cable can carry the bit stream between network devices.

topics.title: Physical Layer Devices
topics.learn: The notes identify cables, hubs and repeaters as devices associated with the Physical Layer.
topics.example: A repeater regenerates weakened signals on a physical medium.

topics.title: Encoding, Decoding and Signal Transmission
topics.learn: Encoding converts data into signals suitable for transmission, while decoding converts received signals into data. Signals can travel through wires, fiber optics or air.
topics.example: Digital data can be encoded into an electrical or optical signal for transmission.

topics.title: Modulation and Demodulation
topics.learn: Modulation changes a carrier signal to encode data, while demodulation recovers the original information. A modem performs these operations.
topics.example: A modem converts data between suitable carrier signals and original data.

topics.title: Point-to-Point and Multipoint Connections
topics.learn: A point-to-point connection directly connects two devices. A multipoint connection allows multiple devices to share one communication link.
topics.example: A direct connection between two devices is point-to-point, while several devices sharing a communication medium form a multipoint arrangement.

topics.title: Unicast, Anycast, Multicast and Broadcast
topics.learn: The notes describe communication from one source to one node, any one node, a subset of nodes, or all nodes respectively.
topics.example: Broadcast sends information to all nodes in a network, while multicast targets a selected group.

chapters.title: Data Link Layer
chapters.description: Frames, MAC addressing, flow control, error control, multiple access and Ethernet.

topics.title: Data Link Layer Basics
topics.learn: The Data Link Layer is the second layer from the bottom of the OSI model and works with frames.
topics.example: Packets received from the Network Layer are encapsulated into frames.

topics.title: LLC and MAC Sublayers
topics.learn: The Logical Link Control sublayer handles flow control and multiplexing, while the MAC sublayer manages access to the physical medium and frame addressing.
topics.example: MAC addressing identifies source and destination devices on a local network.

topics.title: Data Link Layer Services
topics.learn: The notes cover framing, MAC addressing, flow control, error control and access control.
topics.example: A frame contains source and destination MAC addresses for local delivery.

topics.title: Framing
topics.learn: Framing groups raw bits into frames and provides boundaries for node-to-node delivery. Frames contain a flag, header, payload and trailer.
topics.example: The header can contain source and destination MAC addresses while the trailer can contain error-checking information.

topics.title: Fixed and Variable Size Framing
topics.learn: Fixed-size frames use a constant size, while variable-size frames use methods such as length fields or delimiters. Byte stuffing and bit stuffing help avoid delimiter ambiguity.
topics.example: Byte stuffing inserts an extra byte so a data byte is not confused with a control delimiter.

topics.title: MAC Addressing and NIC
topics.learn: A Network Interface Card connects a device to a network, and the MAC address is the hardware identifier associated with the NIC.
topics.example: A laptop's network interface has a MAC address used for local network identification.

topics.title: Stop-and-Wait Flow Control
topics.learn: Stop-and-Wait uses a window size of one. The sender sends one frame and waits for an acknowledgment before sending the next.
topics.example: A sender transmits one frame, waits for ACK and then transmits the next frame.

topics.title: Go-Back-N
topics.learn: Go-Back-N is a sliding-window flow and error control protocol. The sender can send multiple frames, while the receiver sends cumulative acknowledgments.
topics.example: If frame 2 is lost, the sender can retransmit frame 2 and subsequent frames after timeout.

topics.title: Selective Repeat ARQ
topics.learn: Selective Repeat allows multiple frames to be transmitted and acknowledged while retransmitting only lost or damaged frames.
topics.example: If only frame 4 is corrupted, frame 4 can be retransmitted without retransmitting correctly received frames.
keyPoints: Retransmits only missing or corrupted frames

topics.title: Error Detection
topics.learn: The notes cover single-bit parity, checksum and Cyclic Redundancy Check for detecting transmission errors.
topics.example: CRC uses polynomial division to generate a check value.

topics.title: Error Correction and Hamming Code
topics.learn: Backward Error Correction requests retransmission after detecting an error, while Forward Error Correction uses extra information to correct errors without retransmission. Hamming Code is covered as an error-correction technique.
topics.example: Hamming parity bits can help identify the position of an incorrect bit.

topics.title: Random Access Protocols
topics.learn: Random access protocols allow stations to compete for the shared medium. The notes cover ALOHA, Slotted ALOHA and CSMA variants.
topics.example: Two stations transmitting at the same time can produce a collision.

topics.title: 1-Persistent, 0-Persistent and P-Persistent CSMA
topics.learn: The three CSMA access modes differ in how a station behaves when the medium is idle or busy.
topics.example: P-Persistent CSMA transmits with probability p when the channel is idle.

topics.title: CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA
topics.learn: CSMA/CD detects collisions during transmission, while CSMA/CA uses sensing, interframe spacing, contention windows and acknowledgments to reduce collisions.
topics.example: CSMA/CA uses a random backoff period before transmission.

topics.title: Controlled Access Protocols
topics.learn: Controlled access regulates who can transmit on a shared channel using reservation, polling or token passing.
topics.example: In token passing, only the device holding the token transmits.

topics.title: FDMA, TDMA and CDMA
topics.learn: Channelization divides the shared medium using frequency, time or unique codes.
topics.example: FDMA allocates different frequency bands while TDMA allocates time slots.

topics.title: Ethernet Frame Format
topics.learn: The Ethernet frame includes preamble, Start Frame Delimiter, destination address, source address, length/type information, payload and CRC.
topics.example: The destination address identifies the receiving MAC address while CRC checks for corruption.

chapters.title: Network Layer
chapters.description: IP addressing, subnetting, IPv4/IPv6, routing, ARP and NAT.

topics.title: Network Layer Basics
topics.learn: The Network Layer is the third layer from the bottom and works with packets. It handles routing, logical addressing, forwarding and packet-related operations.
topics.example: A router uses destination IP information to forward packets toward another network.

topics.title: IP Addressing
topics.learn: IP addresses identify devices on networks. The notes cover IPv4 and IPv6, along with public and private addressing.
topics.example: An IPv4 address contains 32 bits divided into four 8-bit octets.

topics.title: Classful Addressing
topics.learn: Classful IPv4 addressing divides addresses into classes A, B, C, D and E based on the first octet and uses fixed network and host portions.
topics.example: Class C uses the first three octets as the network portion according to the notes.

topics.title: Subnet Masks, Network ID and Broadcast Address
topics.learn: A subnet mask identifies the network portion of an IP address. The first address is the network ID and the last address can be the broadcast address.
topics.example: For 192.168.1.0/24, the notes identify 192.168.1.0 as the network ID and 192.168.1.255 as the broadcast address.

topics.title: Classless Addressing and CIDR
topics.learn: CIDR improves IP allocation by assigning blocks according to actual requirements rather than fixed classes.
topics.example: 192.168.1.0/28 contains 28 network bits and 4 host bits.

topics.title: Subnetting
topics.learn: Subnetting divides a larger network into smaller networks. Routers can connect different subnets, and host bits can be borrowed to create subnet IDs.
topics.example: Borrowing two bits creates four subnets according to the notes.

topics.title: FLSM and VLSM
topics.learn: FLSM uses the same subnet mask for all subnets, while VLSM uses different masks based on host requirements.
topics.example: VLSM can create larger and smaller subnets from the same address space according to need.

topics.title: IPv4 Header
topics.learn: The IPv4 header includes version, header length, service information, total length, identification, flags, fragment offset, TTL, protocol, checksum and source/destination addresses.
topics.example: TTL limits packet lifetime and helps prevent indefinite routing loops.

topics.title: IPv6 Header
topics.learn: The IPv6 header uses 128-bit addresses and includes fields such as version, traffic class, flow label, payload length, next header and hop limit.
topics.example: IPv6 uses a 128-bit source and destination address.

topics.title: Routing and Routing Tables
topics.learn: Routing selects a path for packets from source to destination. Routing tables contain paths used by routers.
topics.example: A router examines its routing table to choose a next hop.

topics.title: RIP, OSPF and Path Vector Routing
topics.learn: The notes cover distance-vector routing using RIP, link-state routing using OSPF and path-vector routing for inter-domain communication.
topics.example: RIP uses hop count as its metric.

topics.title: Address Resolution Protocol
topics.learn: ARP maps an IP address to a corresponding MAC address within a local network.
topics.example: A device can broadcast an ARP request when the destination MAC address is not present in its cache.

topics.title: Network Address Translation
topics.learn: NAT allows multiple private IP addresses to share public addressing for Internet access by translating IP and port information.
topics.example: A router can translate a private source address into a public address before sending traffic to the Internet.

chapters.title: Transport Layer
chapters.description: Ports, sockets, TCP, UDP, flow control, congestion control and connection management.

topics.title: Transport Layer Basics
topics.learn: The Transport Layer provides end-to-end, process-to-process communication and works with segments.
topics.example: Port numbers allow transport-layer data to reach the correct application.

topics.title: Socket Address
topics.learn: A socket address combines an IP address and a port number so that both the destination device and application can be identified.
topics.example: 192.168.1.10:80 identifies a web service on a particular device.

topics.title: TCP Features
topics.learn: TCP is connection-oriented and provides reliable, ordered delivery with acknowledgments, retransmissions, flow control, congestion control and error detection.
topics.example: TCP can retransmit lost data after detecting that delivery was unsuccessful.

topics.title: TCP Header
topics.learn: The TCP header contains source and destination ports, sequence and acknowledgment numbers, header length, control flags, window size, checksum, urgent pointer and options.
topics.example: The SYN flag is used during connection setup, while ACK confirms receipt.

topics.title: TCP Three-Way Handshake
topics.learn: TCP establishes a connection using SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK.
topics.example: The client sends SYN, the server responds with SYN-ACK, and the client sends the final ACK.

topics.title: TCP Data Transfer and Acknowledgment
topics.learn: TCP uses sequence numbers and acknowledgment numbers to track transmitted and expected bytes. Piggybacking combines data with acknowledgments when possible.
topics.example: An acknowledgment number indicates the next byte expected by the receiver.

topics.title: TCP Window Size and MSS
topics.learn: The receiver window represents the amount of data that can be sent without waiting for acknowledgment. MSS represents the maximum data size in a TCP segment.
topics.example: If the window is 18,000 bytes and MSS is 1,800 bytes, the notes calculate 10 segments.

topics.title: TCP Connection Termination
topics.learn: The notes describe TCP connection termination using FIN and ACK messages and explain both three-step and four-step termination sequences.
topics.example: A client can send FIN, the server acknowledges it, later sends its own FIN, and the client sends the final ACK.

topics.title: UDP
topics.learn: UDP is connectionless, lightweight and fast. It provides no handshake, delivery guarantee, ordering guarantee, flow control or congestion control according to the notes.
topics.example: UDP is associated with time-sensitive, loss-tolerant applications such as streaming, calls and online games.

topics.title: TCP vs UDP
topics.learn: The notes compare TCP and UDP in connection orientation, reliability, error checking, acknowledgments, speed, retransmission, header size and use cases.
topics.example: Web browsing and file transfer are listed with TCP, while video calls, online games, streaming and DNS are associated with UDP.
keyPoints: UDP does not retransmit lost packets

chapters.title: Session Layer
chapters.description: Session establishment, synchronization, dialog management and resynchronization.

topics.title: Session Layer Basics
topics.learn: The Session Layer is responsible for establishing, managing and terminating communication sessions.
topics.example: A session keeps communication between two participating systems organized.

topics.title: Communication Synchronization
topics.learn: The Session Layer can use synchronization points so communication can recover from failures by returning to a known good state.
topics.example: A checkpoint can help resume from a previously synchronized point.

topics.title: Dialog Management
topics.learn: Dialog management controls the direction of communication and supports half-duplex and full-duplex communication modes.
topics.example: In half-duplex communication, a token can determine which side may transmit.

topics.title: Resynchronization
topics.learn: The notes describe Set, Abandon and Restart modes for handling session state after interruptions.
topics.example: Restart can restore a session from a previously saved state.

chapters.title: Presentation Layer
chapters.description: Data translation, compression, encryption, decryption and syntax management.

topics.title: Presentation Layer Basics
topics.learn: The Presentation Layer prepares data in a format that can be correctly interpreted by sender and receiver.
topics.example: The layer can translate data between different representations.

topics.title: Data Translation
topics.learn: Data translation converts data between different formats so systems can communicate using compatible representations.
topics.example: A sender's data representation can be translated into a common format before transmission.

topics.title: Data Compression
topics.learn: Compression reduces the size of data before transmission. The notes distinguish lossy and lossless compression.
topics.example: Lossless compression allows the original data to be restored.

topics.title: Encryption and Decryption
topics.learn: Encryption converts data into an unreadable representation, while decryption converts it back into a readable form.
topics.example: Encrypted information can be transmitted so unauthorized users cannot directly interpret it.

topics.title: Syntax and Semantics Management
topics.learn: The Presentation Layer can provide common syntax and semantics so communicating systems interpret data consistently.
topics.example: Two systems can exchange data after agreeing on a common representation.

chapters.title: Application Layer
chapters.description: Application protocols including HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, DHCP, FTP, SMTP, POP, IMAP and NFS.

topics.title: Application Layer Basics
topics.learn: The Application Layer is the topmost OSI layer and provides network functionality to users and applications.
topics.example: A browser uses application-layer protocols to communicate with web servers.

topics.title: HTTP
topics.learn: HTTP is the HyperText Transfer Protocol used for web communication. The notes describe it as stateless and associated with TCP port 80.
topics.example: A browser sends an HTTP request for a web page and receives an HTTP response.

topics.title: HTTPS
topics.learn: HTTPS is the secure form of HTTP and uses TLS to protect communication. The notes associate it with port 443.
topics.example: Online banking and secure web applications commonly use HTTPS.

topics.title: DNS
topics.learn: The Domain Name System maps domain names to IP addresses.
topics.example: A browser can resolve a domain name such as a website address to an IP before establishing communication.

topics.title: DNS Hierarchy
topics.learn: The notes describe root servers, TLD servers and authoritative servers as parts of DNS resolution.
topics.example: A resolver can contact the root, then the relevant TLD server, and finally the authoritative server.

topics.title: Recursive and Iterative DNS Queries
topics.learn: Recursive resolution allows the resolver to complete the lookup, while iterative resolution involves the resolver receiving referrals and continuing the lookup.
topics.example: A resolver can query a root server, receive a TLD referral, then query the TLD server.

topics.title: DHCP
topics.learn: DHCP automatically provides IP addresses and other network configuration information to devices.
topics.example: A device connecting to Wi-Fi can receive an IP configuration from a DHCP server.

topics.title: FTP
topics.learn: FTP transfers files between hosts and uses separate control and data channels according to the notes.
topics.example: An FTP client can upload website files to a remote server.

topics.title: SMTP, POP and IMAP
topics.learn: SMTP is used for sending email, POP pulls email from a server, and IMAP keeps email synchronized with the server.
topics.example: A mail client may use SMTP to send an email and IMAP to keep inbox state synchronized across devices.

topics.title: Network File System
topics.learn: NFS allows remote hosts to mount and interact with file systems as though they were local.
topics.example: A developer can mount a remote Linux directory and access shared project files.

topics.title: Persistent and Non-Persistent HTTP
topics.learn: Persistent HTTP keeps the connection open for further objects, while non-persistent HTTP closes the connection after the response.
topics.example: Persistent communication can reduce connection overhead when multiple objects are requested.

chapters.title: Delays
chapters.description: Transmission, propagation, queueing, processing and total network delay.

topics.title: Transmission Delay
topics.learn: Transmission delay is the time required to push all bits of a packet onto the transmission medium. The notes give Tt = L/B.
topics.example: For a 20-bit packet on a 1 bps link, transmission delay is 20 seconds.

topics.title: Propagation Delay
topics.learn: Propagation delay is the time taken for a bit to travel from sender to receiver through the medium. The notes give Tp = Distance/Velocity.
topics.example: Increasing the physical distance generally increases propagation delay.

topics.title: Queueing Delay
topics.learn: Queueing delay is the time a packet waits in a buffer before being processed or transmitted.
topics.example: Heavy traffic can create a longer queue and increase queueing delay.

topics.title: Processing Delay
topics.learn: Processing delay is the time used by a router or destination system to inspect and process a packet.
topics.example: A router may inspect headers and update TTL before forwarding a packet.

topics.title: Total Network Delay
topics.learn: Total delay is the sum of transmission, propagation, processing and queueing delays.
topics.example: Ttotal = Tt + Tp + Tpro + Tq. In an ideal case where processing and queueing are negligible, Ttotal = Tt + Tp.
